p: along the lines of what they said
the One Who spoke and the world came to be
that Haman would in the future weigh out shekalim
therefore He put their shekalim before his," etc.
And seemingly, what connection is there
between the shekalim of Yisrael, which are for the Mikdash,
But the essence of the kelipah of Esav
is that he wants to disguise himself,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [בְּרֵאשִׁית כה, כח] כִּי צַיִד בְּפִיו
as it is said (Bereishis 25:28), "for there was trapping in his mouth,"
And he would say to him, 'In the beis medrash.
and is this not its permission?'"
And so regarding the future it is brought
He wraps himself in his tallis like an elder
and comes and sits beside Yaakov,
'Though you set your nest among the stars' —
and 'stars' means none other than Yisrael," etc.
And with this Amalek accuses Yisrael,
claiming they are equal, chas v'shalom.
And so we find with Bilam,
who was also like Amalek, as is known
and he said, "I have arranged the seven altars"
and on the contrary, he offers corresponding to them all.
And what did Hashem Yisbarach answer him?
a minchah mixed with oil, or dry —
"than a house full of feasts of strife" —
for you want to bring strife
that Yisrael act from generosity of heart
and from love of Hashem Yisbarach
that is planted in the depth of their heart,
which is not so with the offerings of Bilam,
chas v'shalom, His will, may He be blessed,
And so was the matter of Haman,
as we say in the Gemara (Megillah ibid.):
"There was none who knew how to slander like Haman" —
meaning he was skilled and expert
for all his accusation was aimed at Heaven,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [מְגִילָּה שָׁם] יְשֵׁנוּ מִן הַמִּצְוֹת
as they said (Megillah ibid.): "They sleep from the mitzvos";
And such was the matter of the shekalim,
as he said, "And ten thousand talents of silver
that wherever it says in this Megillah
it serves both the holy and the mundane;
the King of kings of kings,
And this is according to what they said
"And Esav, he is gracious to the poor," etc.;
and builds public bathhouses from it," etc.,
so that it should be for the needs of the poor,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה [קֹהֶלֶת רַבָּה ד, ה]
and as they said in Midrash Rabbah (Koheles Rabbah 4:5):
"and as the parable goes: she whores for apples
and distributes them to the sick."
it would not have been proper
to put into the treasury money
that he received as the price of an entire nation;
he would distribute it to the poor
or would provide for public needs,
so that it be for the needs of the poor,
in weighing out ten thousand talents of silver,
which matches the number of the shekalim of Yisrael
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּחִזְקוּנִי שְׁמוֹת ל, יד)
and as the Chizkuni writes, Shemos 30:14):
And he would give it to Achashveirosh,
and Achashveirosh would distribute it to the poor;
and this is "to bring into the king's treasuries,"
that he would give to Achashveirosh
and Achashveirosh would give it to charity.
And one may say that it alludes,
עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת י, ב)
"Through what will the horn of Yisrael be raised?
Through 'When you raise up the head.'"
the horn of Yisrael is raised up to the head,
for they are bound to the root.
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בְּרַשִׁ״י [שָׁם דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל אָמַר]
'his horn shall be raised in honor.'"
That is, according to what they said
"In the future Hakadosh Baruch Hu will make
shade and canopies for the masters of mitzvos
beside the sons of Torah," etc.
And this is "his horn shall be raised":
"in honor" — beside the sons of Torah,
along the lines of what they said (Chullin 133a):
And this is the holiness of Shabbos,
which is the revelation of Atika
and this is "in My treasure house."
And Haman said that he too could
and his horn would be raised by it, chas v'shalom.
the shekalim of Yisrael before his,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב קכח, א)
דְּיִתְרְעֵי בֵּיהּ קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וְכוּלֵּי
in whom Hakadosh Baruch Hu takes delight," etc.
And about them it is said,
that the horn of Yisrael is raised
through the shekalim, in its literal sense,
or through charity, as Rashi explains,
and as is evident from the sequence of the topic
'his horn shall be raised in honor,'"
(as they said in Bava Basra there),
for they give from generosity of heart
and from love of Hashem Yisbarach,
and their horn is raised in honor.
Which is not so with "but the kindness of the nations," etc.,
to aggrandize themselves and to boast and the like,
as they said in the Gemara (Bava Basra ibid.).
pleasing sacrifices to the God of Heaven
and he had faith in Hashem Yisbarach —
and in such a case with a Jew,
for Koresh intended nothing at all
וְקָרֵי לֵיהּ בַּגְּמָרָא (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה ג, ב)
and the Gemara calls him (Rosh Hashanah 3b),
on account of this, "after he soured."
And this is like what was answered
And regarding the shekalim for the Mishkan it is explicit:
that the love of Hashem Yisbarach dwells in his heart,
for He is the heart of Yisrael,
as they said in the holy Zohar (there).
And this is the meaning of His putting
even though his shekalim too were for charity,
that his intent was to defy the will of Hashem Yisbarach,
to stand in brazenness like Bilam,
against His will, may He be blessed.
And so at the third meal of Shabbos,
דְּעַתִּיקָא קַדִּישָׁא [זֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בְּאִדְּרָא חֵלֶק ג קכט, א–ב]
as His treasure, without any reason,
only that He testifies to the heart of Yisrael,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [מַלְאָכִי א, ב] וָאֹהַב אֶת יַעֲקֹב
as it is said (Malachi 1:2), "And I loved Yaakov."
And therefore we say (in the zemer Bnei Heichala):
"They are cast outside and do not enter,
that they cannot enter at all:
who are the kelipah of the dog,
and the dogs are brazen of soul,
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב סה, א)
כִּי מִי יוּכַל לָבוֹא אֶל הַמֶּלֶךְ
for who can come before the King
to stir up strife and hatred against His children?

paragraphs.text: Megillah 13b:20–21 — “‘Ten thousand talents of silver I will weigh out.’ Resh Lakish said: It was revealed and known before the One who spoke and the world came into being that Haman would in the future weigh out shekels against Israel. Therefore He caused their shekels to precede his shekels. This is what we learned: On the first of Adar public announcements are made concerning the shekels and mixed species.” Israel’s contribution precedes Haman’s payment in the order of the year and in the divine preparation for deliverance.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Toldot 8 — “When Esav came from outside, he told his father: Father, is salt liable to the tithe? Yitzchak marveled and said: See how particular my son is in commandments. His father asked him: My son, where were you today? He answered: In the house of study. Is this not the law of such and such? Is this not its prohibition? Is this not its permission? Through these words he hunted him with his mouth, and therefore he loved him. But the holy spirit cries: Though he makes his voice gracious, do not believe him, for seven abominations are in his heart.” Esau’s performance imitates Torah devotion in speech. This is the precedent for the apparent equivalence Rav Tzadok sees in the offerings of Bilam and the money of Haman.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Tzav 2 — “In the world to come, when the Holy One, blessed be He, exacts payment from Esau, what does Esau do? He wraps himself in his tallit like an elder and comes and sits beside Jacob. From where? For it is written, ‘Though you place your nest among the stars’; and the stars mean Israel, as it is said, ‘Look, please, toward heaven,’ and ‘So shall your offspring be.’ What does Jacob say to him? My brother, you will not be a brother like me. ... Once Esau departs from the world, the Holy One and Israel remain, as it is said, ‘One is My dove, My perfect one.’” The tallit is a claim to shared identity; the Midrash ends by distinguishing Israel’s particular bond.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 194a, Balak 12:6 — “He sent to Bilam and said to him: I have in me two letters of Amalek—lamed-kuf, the ending of Amalek. ... Rabbi Shimon said: Say it this way: the beginning of Balak is bet-lamed, and the beginning of Bilam is bet-lamed. The beginning of Balak was in Bilam; the end of Amalek was in Balak; and the end of Bilam was the beginning of Amalek.” The names Bilam and Balak jointly contain the letters of Amalek. The source gives a specific symbolic identification rather than merely a general resemblance.

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar Rabbah 20:18 — “Why seven altars? Corresponding to seven altars built by seven righteous men from Adam to Moses and accepted: Adam, Abel, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses. He was saying: Why did You accept these? Was it not because of the service they performed before You? Is it not fitting for You to be served by seventy nations rather than one nation? The holy spirit answered him: ‘Better a dry morsel’—better a meal offering mixed with oil, and dry—‘than a house full of sacrifices of strife,’ for you wish to introduce strife between Me and Israel. ... He said, ‘The seven altars I have arranged.’ ... He answered him: ‘Better a meal of vegetables’—better the meal Israel made in Egypt, eating unleavened bread and bitter herbs—than the bulls you offer through hatred.” The Midrash explicitly contrasts the intention of the offerings. Rav Tzadok develops its distinction between love and the wish to separate God from Israel.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 13b:16–17 — “Rava said: There was no one who knew how to speak maliciously like Haman. He said to him: Come, let us destroy them. He answered: I fear their God, lest He do to me what He did to earlier rulers. Haman said: ‘There is’—they have fallen asleep with respect to the commandments. He answered: There are rabbis among them. Haman said: They are one people.” Rav Tzadok reads this exchange as Haman’s effort to press an accusation against the whole people, including the learned.

paragraphs.text: Esther Rabbah 3:10 — “Rabbi Yudan and Rabbi Levi said in the name of Rabbi Yohanan: Every place in this Megillah where ‘King Ahasuerus’ is said, Scripture speaks of King Ahasuerus; every place where it says simply ‘the king,’ it serves both the sacred and the ordinary meaning.” The rule allows the human king’s treasury to be interpreted simultaneously in relation to the divine King. The statement concerns interpretive levels, not an assertion that Haman consciously intended a sacred gift.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 109a, Behar 5:8 — “Rabbi Shimon said: But we find ‘courts’ in the verse, ‘She stood in the inner court of the king’s house, opposite the king’s house.’ In every place, ‘the king’ without qualification is the Holy One, blessed be He. ‘She stood’—standing means prayer. ‘Opposite the king’s house’—opposite the Temple, for all Israel must direct their prayer there and be opposite the Temple.” The Zohar supplies the same sacred reading of the unqualified title in Esther, here in the scene of Esther’s prayer.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Mishpatim 14 — “‘He who increases his wealth through interest and increase gathers it for one who is gracious to the poor’—this is Esau. Is Esau gracious to the poor? He oppresses the poor! Rather, the government hears that a man is taking interest, brings a charge against him, takes his wealth, and builds public buildings, bathhouses, colonnades in the province, and facilities needed by travelers. Thus, ‘he gathers it for one who is gracious to the poor.’” The Midrash’s provocative designation refers to the public use of confiscated wealth. Rav Tzadok uses it to distinguish an outward charitable result from the donor’s inner intention.

paragraphs.text: Kohelet Rabbah 4:6 — “Another interpretation: ‘Better one handful of rest’—better one who gives a little charity from his own property than one who robs, takes by force, and oppresses, and then gives great amounts of charity from the property of others. The proverb says: She commits adultery for apples and distributes them to the sick. ‘And pursuit of wind’—his desire is to be called a man of good deeds.” The exact proverb occurs in the present division at Kohelet Rabbah 4:6, rather than 4:5. paragraphs.text: Tosafot, Megillah 16a, s.v. “ve-dahi” — “‘And it pushed aside ten thousand talents of silver’—I heard that ten thousand talents of silver amount to half a shekel for each one of Israel, who numbered six hundred thousand when they left Egypt. He said that he would give Ahasuerus the entire price of their redemption. Examine it and you will find it.” Tosafot gives the traditional correspondence but leaves the calculation to the reader. Chizkuni, Exodus 30:14, develops a lifetime calculation; the two presentations should not be conflated.

paragraphs.text: Chizkuni, Exodus 30:14 — “The total of all of them comes to ten thousand talents of silver. How? Most people live only seventy years; subtract twenty years of exemption ... fifty years remain in which each Israelite gives a common maneh, at a half holy shekel each year. Thus sixty people give sixty maneh in their lifetimes, which is a talent. They were six hundred thousand, so all of them together give ten thousand talents. Therefore the wicked Haman said, ‘Ten thousand talents of silver I will weigh out’: He said, My shekels are sufficient to cancel their shekels, and I will give the equivalent of the six hundred thousand among them, to do with them as I wish.” Chizkuni’s comparison uses fifty years of annual contributions, rather than one annual collection.

paragraphs.text: Bava Batra 10b:3–4; Rashi, s.v. “amar lo be-khi tissa” — “Rabbi Abbahu also said: They asked Solomon son of David, How far does the power of charity extend? He said to them: Go and see what my father David explained: ‘He distributed, he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn will be raised in honor.’” Rashi explains the first answer: “If you come to raise their heads in elevation, take from them a ransom for charity.” Thus the Talmudic sequence itself links lifting the head with charity.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 25:2 — “Rabbi Huna and Rabbi Jeremiah said in the name of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba: In the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will make shelter and canopies for those who perform commandments beside those devoted to Torah in the Garden of Eden. There are three verses for this: ‘For in the shelter of wisdom is the shelter of money’; ‘Happy is the person who does this’; and ‘She is a tree of life to those who uphold her.’ ... Because Azariah engaged in business and placed food in Shimon’s mouth, the teaching was called by his name.” The accompanying example concerns material support for Torah study. The promised proximity to scholars explains Rav Tzadok’s reading of elevation “in honor.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Yisrael Kedoshim 10 — “He considered himself a better servant than they: they give only a half-shekel, and he can weigh ten thousand talents… but ‘better a dry morsel with quiet than a house full of quarrelsome sacrifices’… though asleep from the mitzvos, ‘my heart is awake.’” Rav Tzadok there adds the ground of Hashem’s verdict: Yisrael’s true inner will is always to do His will, even when outward deeds fall short.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 128a–b, Terumah 6:5–6 — “‘From every man’—from one who is called a man, who has prevailed over his inclination. Everyone who prevails over his inclination is called a man. ‘Whose heart moves him willingly’—what is meant by ‘whose heart moves him willingly’? One in whom the Holy One, blessed be He, takes pleasure. ... All these expressions speak of the Holy One. paragraphs.text: Bava Batra 10b:7–10 — “Rabbi Eliezer answered: ‘Charity raises a nation’—this means Israel. ... ‘The kindness of nations is sin’—all the charity and kindness the nations do is sin for them, for they do it only to make themselves great. ... Is doing so not complete charity? Was it not taught: One who says, ‘This sela is for charity so that my children may live,’ or ‘so that I may merit the world to come,’ is completely righteous? There is no difficulty: here the case is an Israelite, and there a gentile. ... Rabban Gamliel answered: They do it only to exalt themselves; and whoever exalts himself falls into Gehinnom.” These are particular rabbinic interpretations within a discussion of motive. The same page ends with Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai’s teaching that charity atones for the nations, so its several voices should be preserved.

When it is revealed, Israel’s prayers are accepted. When is it revealed? ... At the time of the Shabbat afternoon prayer. ... paragraphs.text: Bnei Heichala, Shabbat third-meal song; Siddur Ashkenaz, Third Meal, Atkinu 6–10 — “Rejoice now, at this hour, in which there is goodwill and no anger. Draw near to me; see my strength, for there are no harsh judgments. Outside they depart and do not enter, those brazen dogs. Behold, I invite the Ancient of Days to the afternoon meal, until they pass away. His will, which He reveals, is to nullify all the husks.” The song itself places the exclusion of the brazen dogs within the afternoon revelation of divine goodwill. Rav Tzadok identifies the excluded force with Amalek through the following Zohar passage.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 65a, Beshalach 32:5 — “‘Sending away the foot of the ox and the donkey’: These are the two crowns of the left to which the nations attach themselves, called ox and donkey. When Israel are worthy, they send them away and they cannot rule over them. Rabbi Abba said: When they join together, people cannot withstand them. Through a person’s acts below, what should not be aroused is aroused. From their combined force emerges what is called dog, the most brazen of them all. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: You said, ‘Is Hashem in our midst or not?’ I therefore hand you over to the dog. Immediately, ‘Amalek came.’” The identification of the brazen dog with Amalek is explicit. Rav Tzadok applies it to the exclusion of Haman and Amalek from the inner Shabbat bond.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefas Emes, Shekalim 5652, s.v. Darshu Chazal — “Charity has the special power of attaching one to the root, as it says, ‘Charity raises a nation, but the kindness of nations is sin.’ This means that when the wicked reach their own root, it is sin—as the Sages said, scattering the wicked benefits them and the world, while gathering them harms them and the world. Thus Haman gave ten thousand shekels, and thereby reached the root of Amalek, ‘the first of nations’; then ‘his end is utter destruction’ was fulfilled in him. The Holy One therefore caused Israel's shekels to come first, for through them they are raised to attach themselves to their root. This is fulfilled every year, as the Sages said: on the first of Adar they announce the shekels and mixed plantings. For Israel's beginning precedes the world, and there no foreign touch exists at all; only through sins did they become mixed among the nations. Through the shekels they return to attachment to that first root and become separated from the mixture. … The wicked wish to extinguish Israel's attachment to the Holy One, and also wish to intermingle with them. Through the shekels love for Israel is awakened, and all workers of iniquity are separated.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: This passage addresses the apparent equivalence of Haman's money and Israel's money at precisely the level developed here: a gift's power to raise its giver to the root. Sefas Emes argues that the same movement has opposite results, because Haman's root is Amalek, while Israel's prior root is the particular bond in which no foreign claim can enter. This illuminates why matching the amount or outward charitable result cannot purchase the love disclosed at the third Shabbos meal. The emphasis differs from the earlier Sefas Emes note on equal love within Israel: here the issue is the failure of Haman's competing claim.
